articles.title: A bronze cup made near Hadrian’s Wall was found in Spain nearly 1,900 years later; researchers think a Roman soldier may have carried it home as a souvenir
articles.summary: A bronze cup found in a field in central Spain may have been a Roman soldier’s keepsake from Britain about 1,900 years ago.
articles.body: A bronze cup found in a field in central Spain may have been a Roman soldier’s keepsake from Britain about 1,900 years ago. The vessel was found in the village of Berlanga de Duero and measures 4.5 inches wide, 3.2 inches tall, and just a twentieth of an inch thick. Its enamel decoration shows a series of fortifications along the base, while four forts from Hadrian’s Wall are named around the rim.According to Archaeology Magazine, researchers believe the cup was made in the mid-second century A.D., in northern Britain near the wall. Its owner may have belonged to the Cohors I Celtiberorum, a Roman military unit that originated in the Berlanga area and served along Hadrian’s Wall during the late first and second centuries A.D.What does the bronze cup reveal about a Roman soldier’s journey to SpainResearchers believe the bronze cup was a memento brought home from Britain by a Roman soldier. The vessel was found in a field in Berlanga de Duero, a village in central Spain. It is 4.5 inches wide, 3.2 inches tall, and only a twentieth of an inch thick.Along its base, enamel depicts a series of fortifications. Four forts from Hadrian’s Wall are named around the rim that are Condercum, Vindobala, Onno, and Cilurnum. The cup is one of several known vessels portraying the wall’s forts that have been found in the last few centuries. However, it is the first known example to name forts from the eastern section of Hadrian’s Wall.What do the forts reveal about the bronze cup’s ageThe cup’s style and the forts named on it led researchers to date its production to the mid-second century A.D. One of the forts listed around the rim, Condercum, was completed in A.D. 130. Two others, Vindobala and Onno, were destroyed by fire towards the end of the second century A.D.The fourth fort was Cilurnum. Together, these details link the cup’s decoration to the history of Hadrian’s Wall and its forts. Researchers also analysed lead isotopes in the cup and its enamel decoration. The results indicate that the vessel was made in northern Britain, near Hadrian’s Wall, rather than in central Spain, where it was later found.A Roman soldier may have carried the cup back to SpainResearchers believe the cup’s owner was likely part of a Roman military unit, possibly the Cohors I Celtiberorum. The unit originated in the Berlanga area and was stationed along Hadrian’s Wall during the late first and second centuries A.D. This connection provides a possible route for the vessel from northern Britain to central Spain.Archaeologist Jesús García Sánchez of the Archaeological Institute of Mérida says, “We think the cup was customized by the person who was going to have it, and the decoration was related to his experience during his military life.”“The inclusion of the forts’ names made it a very nice souvenir to bring back home.”The cup connects Hadrian’s Wall to Roman SpainThe bronze vessel is notable as the first of its kind to name forts from the eastern section of Hadrian's Wall. Enamel fortifications run along its base, and the names of four Hadrian's Wall forts appear around its rim, while isotope analysis points to northern Britain as the place where the cup was made.Researchers believe it dates to the mid-second century A.D., after Condercum was completed in A.D. 130 but before Vindobala and Onno were destroyed by fire at the end of the second century A.D.The cup was later found in Berlanga de Duero, where its possible connection to the Cohors I Celtiberorum links the vessel to a Roman military unit stationed along the wall.You use AI every day. articles.title: A British collector paid under £100 for a damaged wooden pendant at a provincial auction; experts identified it as rare Rapa Nui jewellery and it later sold for £75,800 including fees
articles.summary: A British collector's under £100 purchase of a damaged Rapa Nui pendant turns into a £75,800 sale after experts identify its rare ceremonial significance. Discover more about this stunning auction find and its cultural history.
articles.body: A damaged wooden pendant bought for less than £100 at a provincial auction has sold for £75,800 after specialists identified it as a rare piece of Rapa Nui ceremonial jewellery.The collector spotted the 10.5-inch object at a UK auction house about eight months before its resale. He placed a low opening bid and secured it without competition because no other bidders showed interest.The buyer later took the pendant to Woolley & Wallis, a specialist auction house in Salisbury, Wiltshire, where experts identified it as a late 18th- or early 19th-century rei miro, a ceremonial ornament from Rapa Nui, also known as Easter Island, The Independent reported.The piece was valued at £10,000 to £20,000 despite missing one of its two heads. A complete rei miro could have been worth up to £600,000, according to auctioneers.Experts identify rare Rapa Nui ornamentThe pendant is a rei miro, a crescent-shaped wooden ornament associated with status and authority on Rapa Nui, a remote Polynesian island in the South Pacific.Rapa Nui is best known for its monumental moai statues and is among the world's most isolated inhabited islands. The island was visited by British explorer Captain James Cook in 1774.The rei miro was part of ceremonial dress and was associated with people of high status. It was reportedly worn mainly by chiefly women but also formed part of the ceremonial regalia of the island's paramount chief, known as the ariki mau.Hardwood was scarce on Rapa Nui, making the material used for these ornaments particularly valuable. The pendants were often carved and polished from driftwood, with their shapes influenced by the timber available.Damaged piece sparks international biddingDespite its missing second head, the pendant attracted strong interest when Woolley & Wallis offered it for sale.The auction house placed its guide price at between £10,000 and £20,000. Instead, bidding pushed the hammer price to £60,000, with fees taking the final amount paid by the buyer to £75,800.A European collector secured the piece, as per the outlet.The final price was 758 times the amount paid by the original buyer in January, turning an inexpensive auction purchase into a substantial return.Woolley & Wallis specialist Luke Hobbs said the original buyer had recognised that the object appeared to be significant even though its importance was not initially identified.“The seller found it at auction in the UK at the beginning of the year. He thought it looked important and ended up buying it for less than £100, so he's made quite a good return,” Hobbs said.He said only a small number of comparable objects had appeared on the market because many were acquired by museums after reaching Britain during the 19th century.Missing head affects valueThe damage had a major effect on the pendant's estimated value.“It is sadly missing one of its heads, or it could have been worth £600,000,” Hobbs said.The auction house has no record explaining when or how the object was brought to Britain.Its original use, however, was clearer. Hobbs said the rei miro would have been worn by people of high status during important ceremonies or festivals.The collector who found the pendant had been interested in tribal art for years. Hobbs described the discovery as a significant moment for the seller.The object joins a small group of surviving Rapa Nui rei miro held in major museum collections. A Rapa Nui wooden rei miro sold for €812,000 at a Christie’s auction in Paris in 2021, according to the auction house.Arts of Africa, Oceania and the Americas specialist Will Hobbs described the latest object as a rare surviving example from one of the world's most remote Pacific cultures.You use AI every day. articles.title: INDIA bloc protests against CEC: 'Unite to fight' proposes Uddhav's Sena; will AAP, DMK relent?
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Should Arvind Kejriwal’s AAP and MK Stalin’s DMK join INDIA bloc’s fight against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over SIR?
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Should Arvind Kejriwal’s AAP and MK Stalin’s DMK join INDIA bloc’s fight against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over SIR? Well, the answer would surely be “yes”, as far as the allies of the bloc are concerned.Now to the more difficult question: Will Arvind Kejriwal’s AAP and MK Stalin’s DMK join INDIA bloc’s fight against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over SIR? Well, there is no straight answer to this one.The AAP and the DMK have a common enemy in the Congress. Uddhav Thackeray’s Shiv Sena (UBT) has now urged the two parties to set aside their differences with the grand-old-party to fight against "dictatorship". In an editorial in the party mouthpiece 'Saamana', Shiv Sena (UBT) said, “The entire country has been witnessing protests against the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), but the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) and the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) have stayed away from it."The absence of both parties, who have officially withdrawn from the INDIA bloc, has highlighted the existing differences within the opposition camp on the strategy and format of the protest against irregularities in the SIR process.'A very critical request'Former Congress leader and senior political commentator Sanjay Jha feels Shiv Sena (UBT)'s suggestion to both the DMK and the Aam Aadmi Party to join the INDIA bloc is a very practical, very reasonable, and at the moment, a very critical request."This is not about, at the moment, anything other than the fact that Indian democracy is in peril. It is unlikely that the CEC is going to resign of his own volition. It is pretty apparent that the government of Mr. Modi is going to be stubborn, and they will stonewall any effort by the opposition to demand and get accountability. Public protests don't seem to make any difference to the government. So the more the merrier," Sanjay Jha says.While the AAP has openly announced it will not be a part of the INDIA bloc’s protest and said “we are fighting this battle in our own way, the DMK has spoken in different tones.DMK spokesperson Saravanan Annadurai accused Rahul of adopting inconsistent positions on the electoral roll revision exercise and questioned why developments in Tamil Nadu had not received the same attention as the broader campaign against the Election Commission.In a post on X, Annadurai called on Rahul Gandhi to clarify his stand on allegations concerning names allegedly removed from Tamil Nadu’s electoral rolls during the SIR process.The DMK spokesperson also referred to a statement attributed to Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge that governments elected after the SIR exercise should be dissolved and sought clarification on why Rahul Gandhi had not publicly endorsed that position and whether such a stand would also apply to Tamil Nadu.Interestingly, a day later, DMK senior leader TKS Elangovan backed Rahul Gandhi on protests against the Election Commission (EC), saying that citizens have a right to protest against the government.“It is the right of citizens to fight against the government’s wrongdoings. That is what Rahul Gandhi did yesterday. Still, this government does not want him to protest because Gyanesh Kumar is being very useful to the BJP. Because of him, the BJP captured power in many states. In all these states, re-elections should be held,” Elangovan said.Will DMK, AAP join SIR protests? The DMK and the Congress had a very unpleasant parting of their two-decade-old ties after the 2026 assembly elections in Tamil Nadu, which the alliance lost to actor-politician C Joseph Vijay’s Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam TVK. While the TVK emerged as the single largest party, it fell short of a majority. The Congress rushed in to help Vijay not just form the government but also eventually join it. Making Congress a part of the government was something the DMK had resisted all along. The Congress move offended the DMK to no end. Since then, MK Stalin’s party has been unrelenting in its attacks on the Congress at all forums from Chennai to Delhi. The Congress, on its part, maintains that it kept the DMK in the loop while shifting loyalties to the TVK.The DMK is missing no opportunity to drive a wedge between the new allies. On Thursday, it lashed out at Chief Minister C Joseph Vijay-led TVK for not explicitly naming the BJP government over the arrest of Congress leader Rahul Gandhi after a protest in the national capital demanding the resignation of CEC Gyanesh Kumar.Questioning the TVK's statement, Elangovan pointed out that it failed to identify the authorities responsible for the action against the leader of the opposition in Lok Sabha. "Who arrested Rahul Gandhi? They should condemn and explicitly mention the name of the BJP government," Elangovan told PTI videos.With the TVK establishing itself as the third pole of Tamil Nadu politics, at least for now, the Congress will have to choose one against the other, and to that extent its ties with the DMK will remain frosty for now. More so, after the TVK has officially joined the INDIA bloc. But the DMK’s measured criticism of the Congress-led INDIA bloc protests may offer a ray of hope to the opposition bloc allies of a future softening of stand by M K Stalin.Now, let’s turn to AAP. Here’s where untangling the strains in the ties may be very difficult, if not impossible. Relations between the Congress and the AAP have always been uneasy and tumultuous. AAP was initially a part of the INDIA bloc.However, ties between Kejriwal’s party and the Congress were never smooth given their competing political interests in several states. AAP attended the first three meetings of the INDIA bloc. The high point in their ties came in the run up to the 2024 Lok Sabha elections when the two parties agreed to a joint contest in Delhi, Haryana, Goa, Punjab and Gujarat.The alliance did not work and the ties ended for all practical purposes after the results were out. In July 2025, Kejriwal formally announced the end of ties.Uddhav Thackeray’s party has reminded Kejriwal of his bitter experiences with Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Union home minister Amit Shah and the Election Commission.“While Kejriwal was the chief minister of Delhi, he was put behind bars in a "false" case. Kejriwal's defeat was engineered by deleting names of voters from his constituency, it alleged. So, it is not in the AAP's interest to stay away from the INDIA bloc,” the Shiv Sena (UBT) wrote in its editorial.'All parties should look at larger picture'Sanjay Jha is confident that these parties will eventually join the opposition protest. He argues it is extremely crucial that the opposition includes everyone.“Whether there are any small, petty differences, whether there is any degree of discomfort with one or the other partner, everyone has to look at the larger picture. And the larger picture is that today people are out on the streets because they're concerned about the future of their vote and the future of democracy,” Sanjay Jha says.“And I believe it is very likely that the DMK and Arvind Kejriwal will join, because this is the time to put aside any petty squabbles and think of the larger goal of the country,” he adds.But this may be easier said than done. The Congress and the AAP are the main rivals in Punjab, where assembly elections are due early next year. The two parties are already engaged in a bitter war of words in Punjab, where AAP is defending its only government and the Congress is going all out to defeat Kejriwal’s party and reclaim its lost glory and government in the state.So, let’s see if this political compulsion decides the future course of ties between the two parties or the “larger goal of the country”?Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Maher predicts 'classic historical a-- whooping' for GOP in midterms but warns DSA could haunt Dems in 2028
articles.summary: Bill Maher predicted a midterm "a-- whooping" for Republicans but warned Democrats face a growing DSA crisis heading into the 2028 election.
articles.body: HBO "Real Time" host Bill Maher predicted during a Sunday appearance on CNN's "Fareed Zakaria GPS" that Republicans would suffer a "classic historical a-- whooping" in the November midterm elections, while warning that the Democratic Socialists of America could create a different problem for Democrats heading into 2028. Maher argued that voters would use the midterms to punish President Donald Trump and Republicans before turning their attention to divisions within the Democratic Party ahead of the next presidential election. "It’s going to be a classic historical a-- whooping," he said. "Now, 2028 is a different story. The Democrats have a crazy animal living in their house called the DSA, and they believe truly insane things. And they’re the energy of the party, and they’re going to make Gaza a genocide, a litmus test, and a lot of other really stupid stuff." BILL MAHER ADMITS HE COULD VOTE FOR JD VANCE, WARNS 'COWARDLY' DEMOCRATS FACE SOCIALIST TAKEOVER The White House rejected Maher’s prediction in a statement to Fox News Digital, pointing to Trump’s support within the Republican Party and arguing the president remained the GOP’s strongest campaign asset. "No one can dispute the fact that President Trump has created one of the most robust coalitions in political history with the MAGA movement, and the President understands how to communicate with them," White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "President Trump is the unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party, and he is committed to maintaining Republican majorities in Congress." Maher attributed the GOP's potential midterm losses to Trump's second-term record, saying that the president had become "drunk with power" and comparing the political dynamic to former President Joe Biden's handling of the Democratic Party's left flank. "Trump screwed the pooch," he said. "That’s what happened. He got drunk with power. This is the pattern in this country. Somebody gets elected. They go way too far with their side of things. Biden did it to a degree with wokeness, and he was too feeble to fight the far left." MIDTERM HISTORY MASSIVELY FAVORS DEMOCRATS. BUT THEY ARE MAKING A BIG MISTAKE "Donald Trump went too far and his party will pay," he continued. The comments came as Republicans face significant polling headwinds with less than a month before Election Day. A Fox News poll found Democrats had a wider path to a House majority, with Democrats projected to win 215 seats compared with 201 for Republicans. That would leave Democrats needing three of the 19 toss-up races to secure a majority, while Republicans would need at least 17. Trump dismissed the polling disadvantage while ramping up his campaign schedule. During a Saturday rally in Vandalia, Ohio, the president argued polling had not accounted for his ability to mobilize voters and urged supporters to approach the midterms as though he was personally on the ballot. REPUBLICANS FACE BRUTAL MIDTERM HEADWINDS. SIX FORCES COULD HELP THEM DEFY HISTORY. The president urged supporters to associate the Republican ticket with his own electoral campaigns. "Just pretend that I’m running," Trump said. "When I run, we win." The Democratic Party's socialist wing scored a series of primary victories and the organization's role in Democratic politics has received increased attention. Rep Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., renewed her DSA membership in August following a seven-year lapse as 2028 speculation continued over either a presidential bid or a challenge to veteran senator Chuck Schumer. "The choice has never been more clear: doubling down on President Trump’s winning, commonsense agenda or the Democrats’ extreme liberal policies and obstruction," he said. articles.title: After visiting 20 African countries, IShowSpeed launched a football fund in 2026 supporting grassroots groups from Ghana and Kenya to Namibia and Rwanda
articles.summary: IShowSpeed’s 2026 African journey did more than produce viral livestreams, packed streets and unforgettable football moments.
articles.body: IShowSpeed’s 2026 African journey did more than produce viral livestreams, packed streets and unforgettable football moments. After travelling across 20 countries during a 28-day tour, the American streamer turned his attention towards something far more lasting. He launched the IShowSpeed Foundation and made its first major campaign the Africa Fund, a football-focused initiative created with Common Goal to support grassroots organisations working with young people. The programme connects his enormous online reach with community football projects across the continent, including organisations in Ghana, Kenya, Namibia and Rwanda.IShowSpeed’s Africa tour became more than a viral journeyWhen IShowSpeed began his African tour, the focus was largely on seeing the continent for himself and showing his audience what he encountered along the way. His 28-day journey eventually covered 20 countries across northern, eastern and southern Africa. He streamed from cities and communities, met supporters, experienced local traditions and attended major football events, including the Africa Cup of Nations final in Morocco.Ghana became one of the most meaningful stops. During his visit, IShowSpeed explored the country’s culture and spoke about discovering his ancestral roots. His trip also included Kenya, Rwanda and Namibia, alongside countries such as Nigeria, Senegal, South Africa, Egypt, Zambia, Angola and Mozambique. The scale of the journey helped expose millions of viewers to places and communities they might otherwise never have encountered through a livestream.The streamer had explained the motivation behind the journey in simple terms: “I want to show the world what Africa really is.”That message became important when the trip ended. Rather than allowing the attention to disappear with the final livestream, IShowSpeed used the momentum to build a charitable project around one of his biggest interests: football.IShowSpeed Foundation launches the Africa FundThe IShowSpeed Foundation was created with a broader goal of increasing young people's access to sport and play. Its first campaign, the Africa Fund, focuses specifically on grassroots football and was launched in partnership with Common Goal. According to the foundation, the programme supports organisations that use football to create opportunities for young people across Africa.The timing was significant. IShowSpeed launched the foundation after experiencing the popularity of football and the strength of local communities first-hand during his tour. Instead of directing the campaign toward major professional clubs or established stars, the fund is designed around organisations already working at community level.Common Goal said the Africa Fund would support African-led football organisations across the 20 countries IShowSpeed had recently visited. IShowSpeed also committed an initial $50,000 of his own money to the campaign, while a wider fundraising drive was opened to supporters.The foundation describes its broader mission as giving young people opportunities to “move, create, and find out what they’re made of.”That distinction matters. Grassroots football is often about much more than producing the next professional player. Local programmes can provide safe spaces, confidence, teamwork, leadership skills and a sense of belonging. The organisations selected for the Africa Fund already have relationships with the communities they serve, giving the initiative a local foundation rather than relying solely on an outside campaign.Grassroots football groups from Ghana to RwandaThe list of organisations supported through the Africa Fund shows how broad the initiative is. The IShowSpeed Foundation names Play Soccer Ghana, Moving the Goalposts in Kenya, PAY Namibia and Umuri Foundation in Rwanda among its supported organisations. It also lists groups working in countries including Côte d’Ivoire, Morocco, Mozambique, Nigeria, South Africa, Zambia and others.Play Soccer Ghana confirmed that it was selected to receive support through the partnership. The organisation says the funding will strengthen its “Play for Fun, Learn for Life” programme, which aims to create safe and inclusive spaces where young people can develop health, resilience and life skills through football.Kenya’s Moving the Goalposts brings another dimension to the campaign. The organisation works with adolescent girls and uses sport to create safe spaces and opportunities for them to learn, lead and develop. Its confirmation of support places the Africa Fund within a wider effort to use football as a tool for social development, not simply recreation.In Rwanda, Umuri Foundation also confirmed its partnership with the IShowSpeed Foundation and Common Goal. The organisation said the support would help improve access to football for young people and reinforce its use of sport as a pathway to opportunity.The foundation's official list also includes PAY Namibia, giving the programme a direct link to one of the final countries visited during IShowSpeed’s African tour.Why IShowSpeed’s football fund could have a lasting impactThe most interesting part of the project may be what happens away from the cameras.IShowSpeed has one of the largest digital audiences in the world, and his African tour demonstrated just how quickly that audience can turn a local moment into a global conversation. His streams brought huge attention to communities, cultures and football fans across the continent. The Africa Fund attempts to convert some of that attention into practical support for organisations already doing the work.That approach also gives the project a different character from a one-off celebrity donation. The foundation has partnered with Common Goal, while the money is directed toward African-led organisations. Those groups understand their own communities and the challenges facing the young people they serve.The foundation's official website lists 16 organisations receiving support through the Africa Fund, covering a wide range of locations and community programmes.For IShowSpeed, the journey therefore did not end when the livestreams stopped. His 20-country African tour created the visibility. The foundation is an attempt to turn that visibility into something that can continue after the cameras move on.Football has always been central to IShowSpeed’s online identity. His passion for the sport has helped him connect with audiences far beyond gaming and streaming. Now, through the Africa Fund, that same connection is being placed behind community programmes where young people can play, learn and build confidence.The bigger test will be measured over time. A successful football fund is not defined by one viral announcement or a large online audience. Its value will be seen in the pitches improved, the young people reached and the local programmes strengthened.For the communities involved, that is where IShowSpeed’s African journey could take on a meaning that lasts far longer than any livestream.You use AI every day. articles.title: 19-year-old student left with no sperm after chemotherapy undergoes UK’s first testicular tissue transplant: Doctors will assess sperm production in eight months; 3,100 worldwide have tissue stored
articles.summary: Doctors in Edinburgh have performed the first testicular tissue transplant in the UK, marking a potential breakthrough in fertility preservation for boys
articles.body: Doctors in Edinburgh have performed the first testicular tissue transplant in the UK, marking a potential breakthrough in fertility preservation for boys and young men who undergo treatments that can permanently damage their ability to produce sperm.According to ITV News, the procedure was carried out on a young man who had his testicular tissue removed and frozen before undergoing intensive chemotherapy as a child. The tissue has now been transplanted back into his body in the hope that it will restore sperm production. The procedure is reportedly only the second such case in the world.Patient left with no sperm after bone marrow transplantThe 19-year-old student, who has chosen to remain anonymous, was left with no sperm in his semen after undergoing a bone marrow transplant to treat a serious blood disorder in 2023. His testicular tissue had been preserved before treatment because chemotherapy can permanently damage the cells responsible for sperm production.Speaking about the procedure, the patient said fertility had been a personal struggle for him for years. He had always hoped to have children of his own but had gradually begun accepting that it might not be possible.“Having this procedure has given me genuine hope for the future. We don’t know yet whether it will work, but knowing that there is now even a possibility means more to me than I can really put into words,” he said.The patient has recovered well and will now be closely monitored. After eight months, doctors plan to remove some of the transplanted tissue and examine it to determine whether sperm production has resumed.How the testicular tissue transplant could restore fertilityThe procedure could eventually provide a fertility option for boys whose testicular tissue has been preserved before they undergo cancer treatment or other therapies that can severely affect fertility.Professor Rod Mitchell, Study Lead and Professor of Developmental Endocrinology at the University of Edinburgh’s Institute for Regeneration and Repair, explained that the preserved tissue can be transplanted either back into the patient's remaining testicle or placed underneath the skin.“The cells that know how to make sperm will start doing that, and we can then take out those sperm and freeze them for the patient,” Mitchell said.However, even if sperm production is successfully restored, patients would still need assisted reproductive treatment. “It means that we would still need to do IVF with the sperm that we created but it would mean that there would be an option for them,” he added.A potential first fertility option for boysFor nearly three decades, ovarian tissue freezing has offered girls undergoing chemotherapy a potential route to preserving their future fertility. Until now, however, boys who undergo fertility-damaging treatment have had considerably fewer options.Mitchell said fertility is often not a priority for children undergoing serious medical treatment. Doctors may discuss the potential impact of chemotherapy with families, but historically there has been little that could be offered beyond preserving the tissue.“When they are young, even if they understand, it's not normally a priority for them at all,” he said.“Then when they come back, five or 10 years later they are suddenly very interested in it and they can then see the benefit of what happened.”The Edinburgh testicular tissue project was established in 2015 with funding from Children with Cancer UK and has since developed into a national programme.Doctors call procedure ‘game changing’Consultant urologist C J Shukla, who carried out the first transplant in Edinburgh during the summer, described the procedure as a privilege but acknowledged that the most important question is whether it will successfully restore sperm production.“I felt privileged that I was able to do the first transplant,” Shukla told ITV News.He said the patient had recovered well without complications, but doctors are now waiting to see whether the transplanted tissue functions as hoped.“What remains now to see is whether it has worked and that's probably a little more nerve wracking,” he said.Shukla also highlighted the pressure involved because the amount of preserved tissue available for each patient is limited.“We have limited tissue per patient and the stakes for the patients are quite high, so you have that one chance of getting it right,” he said.If successful, the treatment could transform fertility prospects for patients who previously had no such option.“The ability to potentially restore their fertility, if it works, this would be game changing for all the patients,” Shukla added.More than 1,200 UK patients have had tissue preservedThe development could potentially benefit a significant number of patients. More than 1,200 people in the UK and around 3,100 worldwide have had testicular tissue stored for possible future clinical use.One of them is Lewis Stevenson from Fife, who was just 11 when he underwent intensive chemotherapy before receiving a bone marrow transplant.Doctors removed and preserved some of his testicular tissue before treatment began. If his fertility has been affected, Stevenson could eventually become eligible for a testicular tissue transplant.Now 20 and a student, Stevenson recalled that fertility was not something he was thinking about while undergoing treatment as a child.“You don't really have an idea of what that intensive treatment is going to be like, so I think my family did a great job of protecting me,” he said.“But it was still a frightening ordeal. Fertility was not on my mind at that age. You're going through the whirlwind of everything that's going on and you're more focussed on just wanting to get better and back to seeing your friends.”‘Now, knowing we have this option to move forward, it’s incredible’As Stevenson grew older, however, the possibility of infertility became increasingly important to him.“It's something you need to think more about. Family becomes really important when thinking about your future. Even having the illness in the first place, then later on you have to worry about your fertility, it's quite distressing,” he said.For Stevenson, the availability of testicular tissue transplantation represents a significant shift from the uncertainty faced by boys who underwent fertility-damaging treatment in the past.“But now, knowing we have this option to move forward, it's incredible,” he said.The Edinburgh procedure is still at an early stage, and doctors will need to establish whether the transplanted tissue can successfully produce sperm. But if it does, the development could mark a major step forward in fertility preservation, giving boys treated for serious illnesses during childhood the possibility of having biological children in adulthood.You use AI every day. articles.title: Researchers built a green-roof test field in Poland; in the hottest months, the planted roof ran up to 24°C cooler than the conventional roof beside it
articles.summary: A study from Warsaw University shows green roofs can reduce surface temperatures by up to 24°C compared to conventional roofs, offering a solution for urban heat management.
articles.body: In cities where concrete, asphalt and dark roofs absorb heat during the day, researchers are exploring whether a layer of vegetation can help buildings cope with rising summer temperatures. Green roofs use plants and growing media to help shield roof surfaces from heat. According to a study by researchers at the Warsaw University of Life Sciences, an extensive green roof in Warsaw, Poland, stayed substantially cooler than a conventional bitumen-covered roof during the hottest months. The researchers compared several small green-roof test plots with a conventional roof under the same outdoor conditions and monitored their thermal behaviour from June to December 2016. During the summer, the difference in surface temperature reached as much as 24°C, while the planted roofs also recorded lower average surface temperatures than the conventional bitumen roof.A small roof field became a natural laboratoryFor the experiment, the scientists built four large green-roof test plots and one conventional roof with a bitumen coating. Each stand measured 2 meters by 1 meter and consisted of layers including waterproofing, drainage, filtration, a 15 cm mineral substrate, and vegetation mats. The vegetation mat initially included moss, sedum and herbs, but after the first year only sedum survived. The test stands were observed from June to December 2016.Seasonal timing was important in the study. The temperature gap was widest during the summer months. The researchers obtained their biggest gaps between June and July, when the maximum temperature gap was 24°C. Their findings were reported in the journal Sustainability in 2019. Average temperature differences were also significant. From June to September, the green roof surfaces averaged approximately 25.7°C to 26.9°C, while the conventional bitumen roof averaged 32.6°C. On one especially hot July day, when the air temperature was 30°C, one green roof averaged 27°C while the conventional roof averaged 52.6°C.Plants changed the way the roof handled heatThe cooling effect was not simply due to the roof’s colour. The plants and growing media changed the way heat and moisture flowed through the roof. A vegetated roof can capture rainwater and store it inside the growing media. As the water evaporates and transpires out of the roof surface, heat is taken away. The Warsaw study showed that rain helped lessen the temperature difference inside the soil after rainy days.According to research published in Applied Energy, extensive green roofs can reduce summer heat loads, with the deeper layers of the growing medium also contributing to the roof’s cooling performance. The Warsaw researchers similarly examined temperatures within the green-roof profile, taking measurements at depths of 3 cm and 15 cm, along with surface temperature, humidity and photosynthetically active radiation. Their findings showed that the thermal behaviour of a green roof depends not only on vegetation but also on rainfall, substrate properties, humidity, solar radiation and the amount of water retained within the roof system.More than a cooler surfaceThe greatest cooling effect occurs on warmer summer days and becomes minimal as temperatures drop. During the winter, the conventional roof may even be cooler than the green roof. However, the experiment showed that vegetation can reduce a roof’s daytime heat absorption. Indeed, a study carried out in Warsaw found a summer maximum temperature difference of 31.3°C between vegetated roofs and their conventional counterparts. For cities with especially hot summers, this technology can be more than decoration: it can act as thermal insulation, a rainwater collector and a regulator of roof temperature. The experiment performed in Warsaw showed that even a small-scale roof covered with plants could create a substantial temperature difference with conventional roofs during hot summer days.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 1964, Lyndon B Johnson signed the Wilderness Act, giving about 9 million acres statutory protection and creating the system that now safeguards wilderness nationwide
articles.summary: Discover the significance of the Wilderness Act signed by President Lyndon B. Johnson in 1964, protecting millions of acres of America's wilderness and forever changing conservation efforts.
articles.body: For much of the 20th century, America's remaining wild landscapes faced a difficult question: could they be kept largely untouched while remaining open for people to experience? The answer came through a new federal system that treated wilderness itself as something worth protecting, rather than simply as land awaiting another use.According to the US Government Publishing Office, President Lyndon B Johnson signed the Wilderness Act on 3 September 1964, permanently protecting about 9 million acres and establishing the National Wilderness Preservation System. The original system contained 54 wilderness areas across 13 states, covering about 9 million acres of national forest land. The Act also established a legal definition of wilderness and set out restrictions intended to preserve its natural character.A new idea of what public land could remainThe creation of the Wilderness Act was a product of lengthy negotiations about the amount of undeveloped American land that should be kept clear of roads and construction. Conservationists pushed for a law to protect these areas from development such as logging and mining. The bill created a mechanism under which Congress, rather than individual agencies, designates wilderness areas. The Act defined wilderness as an area where the earth and its biological community remain largely untouched by humans, where people may visit but do not live.Rather than creating a separate category of federal land, the Act established wilderness as a legal protection that could be applied to existing federal lands managed by different agencies. The Act prohibited commercial activity and the construction of roads in designated wilderness areas, while also restricting the use of motorised and mechanised transport, subject to specific exceptions set out in the law.From 54 areas to a nationwide systemAccording to the Forest History Society, about 9 million acres protected in 1964 were largely areas that the US Forest Service had already classified administratively as wilderness, wild or similar categories. The Wilderness Act gave these places a stronger statutory foundation and brought them into a single National Wilderness Preservation System. Congress has added new wilderness areas through subsequent legislation, extending protection to landscapes across the country.According to the National Park Service, the system now contains more than 800 wilderness areas across 44 states and Puerto Rico. The expansion has brought diverse landscapes into the system, including alpine terrain, deserts, forests, wetlands and beaches. These areas provide protected habitats for wildlife while allowing people to experience places with relatively few signs of modern development. The four federal agencies responsible for managing designated wilderness are the National Park Service, US Forest Service, Bureau of Land Management and US Fish and Wildlife Service, all of which are required to preserve the wilderness character of the areas under their management.A protection system that kept expandingThe act's importance became clearer as Congress added more land to the system. In the 1980s, major laws such as the Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act of 1980 expanded the wilderness system substantially, with the law covering Alaska and adding tens of millions of acres. By 2024, the National Wilderness Preservation System had 806 wilderness areas totalling more than 111 million acres across 44 states and Puerto Rico. This was a long way from the 9 million acres that the Wilderness Act initially protected.The act that Johnson signed in 1964 was far more than just a one-off conservation effort; it was a process that would allow Congress to go on locating and protecting areas of wilderness within America that had remained undeveloped. Sixty years after the Wilderness Act was signed, its core idea still guides the national wilderness system: some public lands have value simply because they are wilderness.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2022, California put plastic from discarded printer cartridges into a 500-foot Highway 99 lane; after thousands of trucks in hot and cold weather, it had no cracking or rutting
articles.summary: Discover how California has innovatively tested asphalt made from recycled printer cartridge plastic, showing promising resistance against cracking and rutting under heavy truck traffic on Highway 99.
articles.body: California tested asphalt that contained recycled plastic from discarded printer toner cartridges on State Route 99 in Elk Grove, south of Sacramento in 2022. The project began with a test on a highway shoulder before the modified asphalt was placed across all lanes of a 500-foot section. Granite Construction later reported that thousands of heavy trucks traveled across the section through hot and cold weather without visible cracking or rutting.The plastic came from printer cartridgesThe recycled material came from used printer toner cartridges, which is a waste stream that can be rather difficult to recycle. Granite Construction worked with researchers from the University of Nevada, Reno to develop an asphalt binder that contained modified toner polymer, or MTP. The mix incorporated 10% recycled plastic by weight of the binder.The highway project conducted an earlier test in a commercial parking lot in 2021, where Granite had used the post-consumer plastic material there before moving to the highway application. The State Route 99 section provided a test under regular traffic, which included heavy trucks and seasonal temperature changes. The work was part of the Cosumnes Bridge Replacement Project in Sacramento County, and researchers were interested in whether the modified asphalt could maintain its performance under conditions that cause conventional pavement to deform or crack.Thousands of trucks crossed the test sectionThousands of heavy trucks were exposed to the Highway 99 section during the field trial, with Granite reporting that the pavement experienced both high temperatures and freezing conditions during the monitoring period. Its 2022 sustainability report said that the section had no cracking or rutting after the early testing period. According to the University of Nevada, Reno, a levee breach flooded the test section during a winter atmospheric-river storm. Researchers inspected the pavement afterward and reported that the plastic-modified asphalt remained intact, despite the additional water exposure and traffic loads. The test therefore gave researchers another set of conditions under which to examine the pavement’s performance.The laboratory work pointed to some changes in the asphalt binder as the amount of toner plastic increased. Granite reported higher stiffness and viscosity in the modified binder, which are properties that can affect how asphalt responds to heat and heavy loading. The researchers were also examining how those changes could influence the material’s resistance to deformation and cracking under different pavement conditions.The test did not establish long-term performanceThe early results were promising, but the Highway 99 project was still a field trial. The University of Nevada, Reno said that researchers continued laboratory and field testing to study the material's long-term resistance to cracking and rutting. Granite also calculated potential environmental benefits from using recycled plastic in asphalt, with its report estimating that the modified mixture could reduce the mix's global warming potential by at least 5% compared with a similar mixture without recycled plastic. Those figures were Granite's calculations for the larger mixture and should not be treated as a measurement of the 500-foot Highway 99 section alone.The project put a waste material from printer cartridges into a conventional road-building application and tested it using regular highway traffic. The early inspection found no visible cracking or rutting after thousands of trucks had crossed the test area, but longer-term monitoring was still needed to determine how the material would perform over a normal pavement life.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2019, Metallica's foundation launched a job-training initiative at 10 US colleges; seven years later, its investment topped $17 million and the programme expanded to 93 colleges across all 50 states
articles.summary: When Metallica launched its Metallica Scholars Initiative in 2019, the programme began with 10 community colleges and a straightforward goal: help
articles.body: When Metallica launched its Metallica Scholars Initiative in 2019, the programme began with 10 community colleges and a straightforward goal: help students gain practical skills for stable, well-paying careers. Seven years later, the initiative has grown into a nationwide workforce education programme supporting 93 colleges across all 50 US states, as well as Guam. All Within My Hands, the charitable foundation created by Metallica’s members and management, says its total investment has now exceeded $17 million. The foundation’s 2026 announcement also revealed its largest annual commitment so far, with more than $3.3 million directed towards the eighth year of the programme. What began as a small experiment in manufacturing education has become one of the band’s most significant efforts beyond music. Read more about it here:Starting with 10 collegesThe Metallica Scholars Initiative was created by All Within My Hands in partnership with the American Association of Community Colleges. According to Metallica’s 2018 announcement, the programme was designed to support students enrolled in career and technical education programmes rather than traditional four-year academic pathways.The first group included 10 community colleges from across the United States. Each college received a $100,000 grant, along with matching support, to strengthen programmes that prepared students for the workforce. The initial focus was largely on manufacturing and related fields, including courses that could lead to jobs in skilled trades and industrial occupations.The foundation’s approach was different from a conventional scholarship that pays only part of a student’s tuition. The grants were provided directly to colleges so they could improve training, support students and make their career programmes more effective. This allowed institutions to address practical needs such as equipment, instruction, mentorship and student services.The first year supported more than 1,000 students. Although the number of participating colleges was small, the programme was built around an area of education that often receives less attention than traditional university study. It recognised that community colleges can provide a direct route into careers that require technical ability, hands-on training and industry knowledge.From manufacturing to wider careersThe initiative expanded steadily after its first year. The Metallica Scholars programme grew from 10 colleges in 2019 to 15 in 2020, 23 in 2021 and 32 in 2022, according to the programme’s official history. Each new stage allowed the foundation to reach more students and include a broader range of career pathways.By the fifth year, the programme was supporting 42 colleges across 33 states. Metallica’s 2023 announcement said the initiative had by then helped more than 6,000 students pursuing careers in the trades. The opportunities were no longer limited mainly to manufacturing, as participating institutions began supporting courses in fields such as welding, automotive technology, industrial technology, construction and other technical occupations.This broader focus reflected changes in the workforce and the needs of individual colleges. Not every community has the same employment opportunities, and students do not all want the same kind of career. By allowing colleges to tailor the funding to local programmes, the initiative could support education that connected more closely with regional industries.The programme also gave skilled trades greater visibility. Many technical careers offer a route to family-sustaining wages without requiring students to take on the cost and time associated with a four-year degree. For students looking for a practical, employment-focused education, that can make community college an important starting point.Reaching all 50 statesIn 2024, the Metallica Scholars Initiative expanded to 60 colleges across all 50 US states and Guam. The development marked a major change from the original programme, which had begun with 10 institutions chosen partly because of their connections to communities visited during Metallica’s US tours.The expansion meant that the initiative was no longer concentrated in a small group of states or regions. Students in different parts of the country could benefit from a programme that supported local community colleges and reflected local workforce needs. In some areas, the focus could be on advanced manufacturing, while in others it could include healthcare, transportation, construction, energy or information technology.Metallica’s involvement also helped bring public attention to community college education. The band is best known for its music, but All Within My Hands has built its charitable work around workforce education, hunger relief and local community services. The scholars programme became a visible example of the foundation using its resources to support long-term opportunity rather than one-time assistance.The biggest expansion yetThe initiative entered its eighth year in 2026 with 18 new colleges joining 75 returning institutions. This brought the number of participating US colleges to 93. According to the foundation’s latest announcement, the programme received more than $3.3 million for the new year, its largest annual grant to date.All Within My Hands said its investment in the initiative had crossed $17 million since its launch. The funding is intended to help colleges improve workforce education and give students the support they need to complete training and move into employment.The 2026 expansion also took the programme beyond the United States for the first time. The foundation committed an additional $250,000, equivalent to approximately £186,000, to establish the Metallica Scholars Initiative in the United Kingdom. This international step suggests that the model could be adapted for community and technical education systems outside the US.Although the number of colleges has grown sharply, the foundation has kept the central purpose of the programme largely unchanged. The initiative continues to focus on students seeking the practical skills required for meaningful and well-paid careers.A different kind of legacyMetallica’s charitable work has developed alongside the band’s decades-long music career, but the Metallica Scholars Initiative has created a legacy that exists far beyond concert venues. Its impact can be seen in classrooms, workshops and training centres where students learn to operate machinery, repair vehicles, build structures or enter other technical professions.The programme does not suggest that every student must follow the same educational route. Instead, it supports a range of options for people who want a faster, more practical path into employment. By investing directly in community colleges, All Within My Hands has helped institutions strengthen the programmes that connect education with local economic needs.Seven years after the launch, the growth is substantial. The initiative has expanded from 10 colleges to 93, reached every US state and attracted more than $17 million in foundation investment. What began as Metallica’s effort to support students entering manufacturing has become a national workforce programme, giving thousands of people a chance to turn technical training into a sustainable career.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'Having productive discussions with Iran': Trump rules out strikes before US midterms
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump said the United States will not attack Iran before the country's midterm elections on November 3, while indicating that
articles.body: US President Donald Trump said the United States will not attack Iran before the country's midterm elections on November 3, while indicating that Washington is engaged in talks with Tehran.“We will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to midterm elections to be held in United States on November 3rd,” Trump said.He also said the United States was holding “productive discussions with Islamic Republic of Iran”.Trump did not provide further details about the discussions or specify what issues were being addressed.Trump’s remarks come despite shipping through the Strait of Hormuz faces growing security risks, with Iran warning that it could block routes it has not authorised.Tankers are facing a higher risk of attacks and intimidation as they try to carry critical shipments through the strategic waterway. Last week saw the highest number of tanker attacks in the Strait since the Iran war began, while the number of vessels attempting to pass through fell to its lowest level in more than two months.Iran has also warned regional countries that any attempt to establish new routes for oil exports would be considered hostile, a senior regional official close to Tehran told Reuters. The official said the policy was part of a plan agreed by Iran’s political leadership and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.“Iran has absolutely no intention of allowing control of the Strait of Hormuz to slip from its hands, and has plans ready to block routes that some regional countries have for exporting oil,” a senior diplomat in the region briefed by Tehran told Reuters.“This could involve missile and drone attacks on ships, or sending boats to scare ships away,” the diplomat added. “It plans to continue this policy of fear and threats,” he said.Tankers seek alternative routesIn recent months, Gulf oil producers have moved shipments through routes closer to the Omani side of the Strait before transferring the oil to vessels in open waters in the Gulf of Oman, with US aerial support, sources told Reuters.The latest incident has raised concerns that the threat could extend beyond the Strait itself. Projectiles struck a tanker about 51 nautical miles off Qatar's coast inside the Gulf in the past 24 hours, the British navy agency UKMTO reported.Maritime security sources said the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged chemical tanker Acers was hit by multiple projectiles north of Qatar's Madinat ash Shamal. The incident caused minor injuries to members of its crew.“The Acers strike raises the prospect of a wider combat area affecting approaches to Qatar, Bahrain, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and Iraq,” maritime risk intelligence group Pole Star Global’s subsidiary Clearwater Dynamics said in a report on Thursday.The vessel's operator, listed in shipping databases as Antigua and Barbuda-based Valvoria Shipping, could not be reached for comment.The attacks have also affected the willingness of shipping companies to use the waterway.“The recent spate of Iranian attacks seems to have dampened the appetite of shipowners to sail through the Strait,” said Jakob Larsen, chief safety and security officer at shipping association BIMCO. “The Iranian threat appears to have increased.”You use AI every day. articles.title: Indian students make extraordinary contributions to our campus, says Indian American President of University of Arizona Suresh Garimella
articles.summary: Suresh Garimella is the President of the University of Arizona and a distinguished professor in the department of mechanical and aerospace engineering.
articles.body: Suresh Garimella is the President of the University of Arizona and a distinguished professor in the department of mechanical and aerospace engineering. Focused on building a strong, aligned leadership team and ensuring long-term financial health for the institution, Garimella has consistently championed student access and affordability.Previously President of the University of Vermont, as well as the Goodson Distinguished Professor of mechanical engineering and executive vice president for research and partnerships at Purdue University, he earned his bachelor’s degree from the Indian Institute of Technology Madras before moving to the US. A highly cited scholar, Dr. Garimella was appointed to the newly established office of science advisory committee for the US Department of Energy earlier this year.In an exclusive interview with Ishani Duttagupta, he discusses his deep connection with the global IIT alumni network, the contribution of Indian students to his university, and more. Edited excerpts:In your role, leading the University of Arizona, what have been the most complex leadership challenges you have faced?Every leader and every university faces moments that test their resilience, but I have found that the most effective leaders remain focused on a clearly articulated mission while bringing people together around a shared vision for the future. Public higher education is changing rapidly. Universities are being asked to prepare students for career paths that are continually and rapidly evolving, accelerate research that addresses society's most pressing challenges and demonstrate their value to the communities they serve. Meeting those expectations requires both disciplined decision-making and the ability to unite people around a common purpose. At the University of Arizona, that has meant making difficult decisions while keeping our eyes firmly on the future. We have strengthened our financial foundation, brought greater focus and discipline to our priorities and positioned the university to build on its considerable strengths. I believe leadership is ultimately about creating the conditions for talented people to succeed. When people understand where an institution is going, how their work contributes and what success looks like, remarkable things become possible.What are the current trends for international student enrolment from India at the University of Arizona? Are numbers fluctuating, and how is the university actively recruiting global talent?India continues to be one of the University of Arizona’s most important international partners, and Indian students make extraordinary contributions to our campus community through their scholarship, research and leadership. Like at many universities, international enrolment naturally fluctuates in response to global conditions, but our long-term commitment to India remains strong. We continue to explore and secure partnerships with Indian institutions and industry, especially building on areas in which we rank at the top in the world. The future of higher education will increasingly be defined by global collaboration. Whether addressing advances in artificial intelligence, health care, water resources and sustainability, or semiconductor manufacturing, universities must work together to prepare the next generation of leaders and solve challenges that no single institution or nation can address alone. That spirit of collaboration is central to our vision at the University of Arizona.A growing number of Indian Americans now lead major US universities. Did your journey as an immigrant present unique institutional or cultural hurdles, and how did you navigate them?Moving to live in another country is an exercise in learning and in adapting. Every institution has its own culture and expectations, but I quickly discovered that curiosity and integrity with a sense of purpose transcend borders. My education at IIT Madras and before, as well as at Ohio State and at the University of California Berkeley, gave me an outstanding technical foundation, and perhaps more importantly, it instilled discipline and a lifelong commitment to learning. Those lessons have stayed with me throughout my career. I have also been fortunate to work alongside exceptional mentors, colleagues and students from many different backgrounds. Those experiences have reinforced my belief that universities are strongest when they bring together people with diverse perspectives in pursuit of shared goals. Some of our greatest innovations, and our greatest opportunities, come through learning from one another.Looking back at your time at IIT Madras, what specific elements of that rigorous educational foundation gave you a competitive edge in your American academic career?IIT Madras challenged us to think critically and take on complexity with confidence. It taught us to remain curious and continue learning throughout our lives. It was a hyper-competitive atmosphere, but perhaps that helped me discover my core strengths and built resilience. My training prepared me well for graduate study in the United States, and it shaped my approach to leadership. Whether in research or university administration, progress begins with asking the right questions and listening carefully. Bringing together talented people with different perspectives is invaluable. The challenges facing higher education, and society more broadly, are increasingly complex. Solving them requires institutions that are willing to innovate, partner strategically and remain focused on uplifting society.AI is rapidly transforming higher education. Do you view it primarily as a disruptive operational challenge for universities, or a tool for academic advancement?Artificial intelligence offers a generational opportunity. As chair of the US Department of Energy’s Genesis AI Mission advisory subcommittee, I would like to emphasize the opportunity and the challenge. Like every transformative technology, AI presents challenges that must be addressed thoughtfully, but it also has tremendous potential to accelerate discovery, improve teaching and prepare students for a rapidly changing workforce. Our responsibility is to help students think critically, apply these technologies ethically and develop the creativity, judgment and leadership that remain uniquely human. Throughout history, universities have helped society navigate periods of profound change. AI is no different. Public research universities have both the opportunity and the responsibility to ensure these technologies are developed and applied with humanity at the core.How do you successfully balance your role as an active researcher and academic with the demanding administrative responsibilities of a major university president?My research and teaching career has fundamentally shaped how I approach leadership. Engineers are trained to ask questions, rely on evidence and solve complex problems collaboratively. Those same habits are invaluable in leading a university. Although I spend less time directly conducting research today, remaining engaged with our faculty, students and research enterprise keeps me connected to the university's core mission. Great public research universities create opportunity. They prepare students to lead, advance discoveries that improve lives and serve as engines of economic growth and societal progress. At the University of Arizona, success for every student is our North Star. My responsibility is to help create an environment where students, faculty and staff can thrive, where discovery translates into opportunity and where our work uplifts the people of Arizona and communities around the world.I also enjoy staying connected with cutting-edge research in my roles providing strategic research leadership through advisory committees for the National Science Foundation, US Department of Energy, and Sandia National Laboratories among others.In what ways do you stay connected to your Indian roots today, and how active are you within the global IIT alumni network?India will always be an important part of who I am. I remain connected through family, lifelong friendships, professional colleagues and the global IIT alumni community. Those relationships continue to be an important part of my personal and professional life. I also value opportunities to remain engaged with higher education leaders across India, including through my role as Chair of the Global Advisory Council for the Confederation of Indian Private Universities. I maintain a longstanding commitment to strengthening collaboration between universities in India and the United States and creating opportunities for institutions to learn from one another.As Arizona’s flagship, land-grant university, we believe our responsibility extends beyond our campus. We are committed to building partnerships that expand educational opportunity, strengthen research and create meaningful impact for the communities we serve. I believe India’s universities will play an increasingly important role in shaping the future of higher education, and I look forward to strengthening those relationships in the years ahead.What do you consider your most impactful achievement or turnaround success since taking office at the University of Arizona?I am deeply proud of what our university community has achieved together. Since coming to the University of Arizona, we have restored financial stability by eliminating the university’s $177 million budget deficit while continuing to invest in our people and keeping resident undergraduate tuition flat for three consecutive years to preserve access and affordability. We implemented a new enrolment management strategy that creates multiple pathways to the university while investing in the academic and well-being programs students need to graduate in four years with minimal debt and pursue strong career opportunities. That commitment includes making counselling services available to students at no cost, removing a financial barrier to care and helping ensure students have the support they need to thrive. We are equally committed to preparing students to succeed in an increasingly interconnected world. One example is the expansion of our Study Abroad program, made possible by a generous $20 million gift from the Garcia Family Foundation. This investment will provide international experiences to students who otherwise might not have had the opportunity to study abroad, broadening their perspectives and better preparing them to lead in a global economy. We continue to build momentum. Our responsibility is to serve as a force for good for Arizona and beyond. That is the work that inspires me every day.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.summary: What began as a nationwide student movement over education funding and poor school conditions has escalated into clashes in the French capital.
articles.body: What began as a nationwide student movement over education funding and poor school conditions has escalated into clashes in the French capital. Students barricaded a high school in northeastern Paris on Thursday, as police fired tear gas as protests showed few signs of easing.The Hélène Boucher high school became the latest flashpoint in the unrest as students used rubbish bins to block its entrance and riot police gathered in nearby streets. The confrontation came as hundreds of high school and university students took to the streets in Paris, with a major demonstration planned from Place de la République towards Place de la Bastille.The latest escalation came after days of disruption across France. More than 6,600 people have been arrested since late September, when mostly under-18 students began protesting over education funding and conditions in schools, according to the Interior Ministry. The Education Ministry said 375 schools were fully or partially closed on Thursday.At least a dozen demonstrations supporting the student movement were also planned across France on Thursday, underlining the widening scale of the protests.Many protesters in Paris wore surgical masks or hoodies, apparently to avoid being identified. As the crowd gathered near Hélène Boucher, police surrounded a nearby square and fired tear gas after protesters surged.Anger over schools, police responseThe protests have been driven by complaints over underfunded schools, ageing facilities and staff shortages. But the movement has also drawn trade unions and political groups, as well as troublemakers whose actions have led to clashes and damage.Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu sought to condemn the violence in a televised address, citing attacks on students and staff, injuries to police officers and gendarmes, and schools being set on fire or vandalized.“We cannot play with the safety of France’s youth,” Lecornu said.He also criticised “political leaders who use this anger to conduct their electoral battles.” France is due to hold a presidential election in April.At Place de la République, smoke from burning rubbish hung in the air as students prepared to march towards Bastille. Protesters carried signs bearing their schools’ names and placards reading “More money for repression than for our education” and “Who protects us from the police?”“We’re here, we’re demonstrating, and we won’t stop. Until October, November, December if necessary. Nothing will stop us,” said Sofia Ferdials, 18, a student at Paris 8 University.Students say protests will continueThe unrest has raised concerns over both school conditions and the police response. Emma Khelil, an 18-year-old university student who returned to her former high school to support the protesters, said she was worried about police violence.“We’re here to defend our rights, not to lose an eye or a hand,” Khelil said.She said she had seen insulation problems and water leaks at the school and had occasionally seen rats.Khelil also rejected the idea that the government's response would end the movement.“I don’t think the movement is going to lose momentum. As long as things don’t change, we’re going to see the movement grow stronger, and potentially a convergence of struggles, especially with the next presidential election coming up,” she said.Dounia Gergeon, a 39-year-old school librarian who joined the Bastille demonstration, said young people felt increasingly unsupported.“They do not feel supported,” she said. “They feel cornered and forced to work under these conditions.”Unrest spreads beyond FranceThe protests have also inspired student unrest in Belgium and Italy.In Belgium, authorities in Liege banned public gatherings until midnight on October 16 after clashes involving several hundred protesters. Police used water cannon and tear gas on Wednesday, nearly 90 people were arrested and several officers were injured.The Belgian protests include demands for more teachers and smaller classes, as well as opposition to education reforms. Protesters have also referred directly to the events in France.In Italy, students have occupied schools and organised marches in several cities. Activists have invoked the French movement with the slogan “let’s do as they do in France”.In Turin, students occupied several high schools over building conditions, education funding and increased military spending. In Rome, students occupied one school and walked out of another, while students in Naples also protested against a planned migrant detention centre.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: In 2022, Washington replaced conventional riverbank defenses with engineered log structures and native plants; early tests showed the approach could protect banks while improving habitat
articles.summary: Discover how Washington implemented a novel approach to combat riverbank erosion in 2022 by using engineered log structures and native plants to enhance habitat for wildlife while protecting riverbanks.
articles.body: Washington tested a different way to deal with eroding riverbanks in 2022, where crews used timber structures, willow plantings and other native vegetation at two pilot sites in the Chehalis River Basin instead of having to rely only on conventional bank protection. The projects were designed to slow erosion while also improving conditions for salmon and other wildlife.One site was along the Satsop River near Brady, where erosion had been eating into riparian forest and farmland for years, while another was on the South Fork of the Newaukum River near State Route 508, where the river had moved toward a home. The two projects used different combinations of vegetation and engineered wood structures.The Satsop River was losing land to erosionThe Satsop River pilot covered a section where bank erosion had been progressing for decades, and Washington's Office of Chehalis Basin said that erosion in the wider project reach had sometimes exceeded 100 feet per year. One landowner had lost about 30 acres of riparian forest and farmland since 1991. The larger restoration plan for the area required engineered log jams and riparian planting, but design and permitting meant that construction would take longer. The conservation district therefore installed an interim planting project in February 2022.Crews put 350 six- to 10-foot cottonwood and willow poles into the ground in two rows that were parallel to the riverbank. They drove the poles between three and eight feet deep, and the deeper plantings were intended to reach groundwater and survive summer drought. By September, about 80% of the poles had survived, and some had produced nearly 10 feet of new growth during the first season. A December 2022 program memorandum described the work as an experimental, low-cost approach that was intended to establish roots quickly while the larger restoration project was being prepared.Logs and plants were used together on the NewaukumOfficials said that the South Fork of the Newaukum River had moved 15 to 20 feet in the previous year and more than 100 feet in recent years near the property by March 2022. Construction took place in September and October, when engineers installed timber structures called cribwall jams and embedded tree trunks and timber piles eight to 11 feet into the bank. They also regraded the upper bank, added coir erosion-control fabric and installed live willow fascines.The planting followed in November, and the site received 25 potted willows, 25 red osier dogwoods, 10 western red cedars, 10 Douglas firs and 100 willow stakes. The project then moved into monitoring, and during a subsequent high-water event, the conservation district reported that the log cribwall appeared to be functioning as designed.The goal was erosion control and habitatThe Chehalis Basin Strategy treats erosion management and aquatic habitat as connected problems, with its program objectives including the need to address urgent erosion threats while protecting or improving habitat conditions. Five pilot projects were completed in the basin before the formal erosion-management program began, and the use of living trees was important because their roots can eventually reinforce the soil along the riverbank. Native vegetation also provides cover and shade, while woody structures can alter local flow and add physical complexity to a river.The larger Satsop restoration plan was intended to benefit four salmonid species, and Washington officials also expected increased habitat complexity to benefit amphibians, waterfowl and other native fish. At Satsop, officials said that more time was needed to determine whether the new root systems would significantly reduce erosion. The engineered log structure had entered monitoring after construction at State Route 508, and the pilots were therefore being used to test whether native vegetation and engineered wood could provide bank protection while serving a broader habitat-restoration purpose.You use AI every day.
